##### **1.3 Uniform Circular Motion and Centripetal Acceleration**

A particle executes **uniform circular motion** when it moves around a circular path or arc of fixed radius $r$ at a constant (*uniform*) speed $v$. Although the scalar speed does not change, the velocity vector $\vec{v}$ continuously changes direction along the tangent to the trajectory. Because velocity is a vector quantity, this directional variation requires an acceleration directed perpendicular to the velocity and pointing toward the center of curvature.

```{tikz}

  \draw[->] (-2.5,0) -- (2.8,0) node[right] {$x$};
  \draw[->] (0,-2.5) -- (0,2.8) node[above] {$y$};
  \draw[gray!60, dashed] (0,0) circle (2);
  \filldraw (1.414, 1.414) circle (1.5pt) node[above right] {$p(x_p, y_p)$};
  \draw[thick, ->] (0,0) -- (1.414, 1.414) node[midway, below right] {$r$};
  \draw[blue, thick, ->] (1.414, 1.414) -- (0.566, 2.262) node[above left] {$\vec{v}$};
  \draw[red, thick, ->] (1.414, 1.414) -- (0.707, 0.707) node[midway, left] {$\vec{a}$};
```

To derive the acceleration vector analytically, consider a particle $p$ at position coordinates $(x_p, y_p)$ lying on a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin, with angle $\theta$ relative to the positive $x$-axis. The position coordinates satisfy $x_p = r \cos\theta$ and $y_p = r \sin\theta$. Because $\vec{v}$ is directed counterclockwise along the tangent line, it forms an angle $\theta$ with the positive vertical direction:

$$\vec{v} = v_x \hat{\imath} + v_y \hat{\jmath} = (-v \sin\theta)\hat{\imath} + (v \cos\theta)\hat{\jmath}$$

Expressing the trigonometric ratios via the coordinates $\sin\theta = y_p / r$ and $\cos\theta = x_p / r$ yields:

$$\vec{v} = \left(-v \frac{y_p}{r}\right)\hat{\imath} + \left(v \frac{x_p}{r}\right)\hat{\jmath}$$

Differentiating $\vec{v}$ with respect to time $t$, noting that speed $v$ and radius $r$ are constant:

$$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \left(-\frac{v}{r}\frac{dy_p}{dt}\right)\hat{\imath} + \left(\frac{v}{r}\frac{dx_p}{dt}\right)\hat{\jmath}$$

The time rates of change of the coordinates are the velocity components themselves: $\frac{dx_p}{dt} = v_x = -v \sin\theta$ and $\frac{dy_p}{dt} = v_y = v \cos\theta$. Substituting these identities produces:

$$\vec{a} = \left(-\frac{v^2}{r}\cos\theta\right)\hat{\imath} + \left(-\frac{v^2}{r}\sin\theta\right)\hat{\jmath} = a_x \hat{\imath} + a_y \hat{\jmath}$$

The magnitude $a$ of this vector follows from the Pythagorean theorem:

$$a = \sqrt{a_x^2 + a_y^2} = \frac{v^2}{r}\sqrt{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta} = \frac{v^2}{r} \tag{1}$$

The direction angle $\phi$ of $\vec{a}$ relative to the horizontal axis satisfies:

$$\tan\phi = \frac{a_y}{a_x} = \frac{-(v^2/r)\sin\theta}{-(v^2/r)\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$$

Because both components $a_x$ and $a_y$ are negative when the particle is in the first quadrant ($x_p > 0, y_p > 0$), the vector $\vec{a}$ points in the direction exactly opposite to the radial position vector $\vec{r}$. Consequently, $\vec{a}$ points radially inward toward the center of curvature at every instant. This acceleration is termed **centripetal acceleration** ("center-seeking").

The time required for the particle to complete one full revolution of circumference $2\pi r$ is the **period of revolution** $T$:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} \tag{2}$$

Solving Eq. (2) for $r = \frac{v T}{2\pi}$ and substituting into Eq. (1) expresses centripetal acceleration in terms of speed and period:

$$a = \frac{2\pi v}{T} \tag{3}$$

* **Worked illustration (high-g turn limits):** An aircraft enters a horizontal turn in uniform circular motion with velocity $\vec{v}_i = (400\hat{\imath} + 500\hat{\jmath})\text{ m/s}$ and leaves the turn $\Delta t = 24\text{ s}$ later with reversed velocity $\vec{v}_f = (-400\hat{\imath} - 500\hat{\jmath})\text{ m/s}$. The constant speed of the turn is:

$$v = \sqrt{400^2 + 500^2} = \sqrt{410000} \approx 640.31\text{ m/s}$$

Because $\vec{v}_f = -\vec{v}_i$, the aircraft has traversed exactly half of the circular orbit in $24\text{ s}$, meaning the full orbital period is $T = 2(24\text{ s}) = 48\text{ s}$. Evaluating the centripetal acceleration using Eq. (3):

$$a = \frac{2\pi(640.31\text{ m/s})}{48\text{ s}} \approx 83.81\text{ m/s}^2 \approx 8.6g$$

In human physiology, centripetal acceleration directed from head to foot displaces blood away from the brain. At $2g$ to $3g$, an occupant experiences significant heaviness; near $4g$, reduced brain perfusion triggers loss of peripheral and color vision ("tunnel vision"); sustained acceleration beyond this threshold induces $g$-LOC ($g$-induced loss of consciousness). The computed $8.6g$ value substantially surpasses the unassisted human tolerance limit.
